measurement.coverage: hits / replicates at level 0.95; a refused replicate counts as not covering and is counted (as C2a). The interval is mean -/+ z se with z the 0.975 normal quantile of each implementation's own arithmetic.
measurement.perReplicate: For every sample each implementation records: refused or not, the associated set at from (riskAtFrom), the number of support points, the mean, the variance and whether the interval contains the truth.
measurement.crossFeedAgreement: Two implementations agree on a sample when: the refusal state is equal; riskAtFrom is equal; the number of support points is equal; |mean_a - mean_b| <= 1e-10 max(1, |mean_b|); |variance_a - variance_b| <= 1e-10 max(1, |variance_b|); and the covering flag is equal. A sample in which either implementation's interval edge lies within 1e-9 of the truth is exempt from the flag comparison only, and every such sample is counted and reported (a flag there is decided by rounding, not by the estimator).
measurement.exactReproduction: F2 and F3 compare hits (coverage times replicates, an integer), the refused count and the median associated set at from with the pinned Part A numbers; equal means equal.

amendments.text: How the per-sample output is pinned, and what a refused sample compares. (1) The per-sample output of an implementation on an ensemble is a table of eight float64 per sample (refused, riskAtFrom, number of support points, mean, variance, interval low, interval high, covered; zeros after the first field for a refused sample). At 24000 rows per implementation the tables stay outside the repository with the sample files, regenerable by seed; a commit pins each by its sha256 together with, per ensemble, the hits, the refused count, the median associated set at from, and the covering and refusal flags of every sample as hex bitmaps (sample r is bit r, the most significant bit of each byte first). The validator checks the sha256 of every table it reads against the pinned one before it compares. (2) For a refused sample only the refusal state is compared: the prototype returns no numbers for one. (3) F1's clause on the prototype module is measured as the git blob id of js/kernels/statistics/truncation.js in the spike's tree being 0414726d99491b3e4106e210d515cbea6d4308b1, its id at 4735488a; and the follow-up's oracle checks that the source text of its gen_truncated and cm_closed is found verbatim in tools/censoring-oracle/oracle.py (sha256 2fb932c306f2b0f5b7df7a170e07597d6d41f9b04033a25265a9e6cdfeafbb7a), recording the result, which F1 requires to be true. No bound is moved.

decisions.text: C2c is run on T1 and on T2, by both implementations, because C2o's statement and bound cover both scenarios ('each in [0.92, 0.98]'): the leg that stands in C2o's place judges everything C2o judged, and the prototype on the same designs. A T2-only miss therefore fails the follow-up although Part A's failure was on T1.

The cross-feed runs in both directions over whole ensembles (Part A's and the new ones), not over a few samples: it then also says, exactly, what each implementation makes of the other's ensemble, so the difference between 0.919 and 0.951 is attributed either to the implementations (a failed XF leg) or to the two sets of draws (both XF legs passing). The oracle reading stream samples is the cross-feed itself; it reads draws, never an estimate.

Whether the two generators draw from the same population is not judged by a bound: the gate document defined no such leg. G1 and G2 report the difference between the ensembles and the pooled coverage so the record can say what the numbers support.

A passing follow-up is recorded as 'A through C2c' by the function above because the register row of Part A's verdict names that outcome; it is a recommendation to Carl in a DELEGATED row and changes nothing that is built, since Part B stays unbegun under the consumers rule.
